Power Supply, Switch, Load: Reading a Simple Circuit

Unit 3: Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 13 of 53 in BMET Academy.

A schematic is not a picture of the inside of a device. It is a map of where current can go. Once you can trace a path on paper you can find the one place the path is broken.

Every circuit has three parts

  1. A source: the battery, the power supply output, the wall outlet. It provides the push.
  2. A control: the switch, relay, or transistor that decides whether the path is complete.
  3. A load: a lamp, a heater, a DC motor in a pump, a speaker, or a circuit board that does the work and uses the power.

Add the wires that join them and you have a circuit. If current is not flowing, exactly one of those four things is at fault, and the meter tells you which.

Switches are the control you meet most, and they are described two ways at once. By feel: a toggle switch flips, a rocker switch tips one end in, a pushbutton switch springs back when you let go, and a membrane keypad is a printed version of the same contact. By what the contacts do: a single-pole switch breaks one conductor while a double-pole switch breaks two at once, which is how a mains switch opens hot and neutral together, and a single-throw switch has one on position while a double-throw switch moves its common contact between two outputs.

Symbols to recognize on sight

cell             one long line and one short line; the long line is positive
battery          several cells stacked, long and short alternating
resistor         a zigzag, or a plain rectangle on newer drawings
lamp             a circle with an X or a loop inside
switch           a line lifted away from a contact
fuse             a loop, or an S, between two terminals
circuit breaker  a switch with a small hook or an arc through it
capacitor        two parallel plates; a curved plate means polarized, so it goes in one way
inductor         a series of loops or humps, like a coil of wire
transformer      two coils facing each other, often with lines between them for the core
diode            a triangle pointing into a bar; current flows the way the triangle points
LED              the same triangle and bar with two small arrows coming off it
ground           three horizontal lines, each shorter than the one above
chassis ground   a small hatched bracket or rake

Crossing versus joining

Two lines that cross with no dot are two wires passing each other with no connection. A dot at the junction means they are joined. Older drawings used a little hop over the crossing wire to say the same thing. Misreading a dot is how a beginner sees a short that is not there.

Following the power path

This is the single most useful skill in the unit. A device is dead; trace the path in order and measure at each step.

  1. The outlet and the cord. Is there voltage at the receptacle, and is the cord intact at both ends?
  2. The plug and the inlet. Many devices have a detachable cord that works loose.
  3. The fuse or breaker. Measure across it: a good fuse has almost no voltage across it, an open one has all of it.
  4. The switch. Across a closed switch you should read almost nothing; the full supply voltage across it means it is open.
  5. The power supply. Does its output rail read the voltage printed beside it?
  6. The load. If the supply is good and the load does nothing, the fault is in the load or in the wiring to it.

You walk the path until the voltage disappears. The part between the point where it is present and the point where it is gone is the part that is broken.

Block diagrams

A block diagram drops the symbols and draws each section as a labeled box with arrows for the signal flow: mains in, power supply, controller, display, motor drive, motor. It will not tell you which component failed, but it tells you which section to put the probes in, and it is the first page you should look at in a service manual for a device you have never opened. Signals are drawn flowing left to right and power top to bottom, so read it that way.

Exam tip: full source voltage across a part that should be a conductor (a fuse, a closed switch, a wire) means that part is open. Near zero volts across it means it is doing its job.
Remember
Source, control, load, and the wires between them. Symbols: battery with the long line positive, resistor zigzag or rectangle, lamp circle with an X, switch lifted line, fuse loop or S, breaker with a hook, capacitor plates (curved means polarized), inductor coils, transformer two coils, diode triangle into a bar, LED with arrows, ground three shrinking lines, chassis a hatched bracket. A dot means joined, no dot means crossing. Trace outlet, cord, plug, fuse, switch, supply, load until the voltage disappears.
Deeper explanation

Power Supply, Switch, Load: Reading a Simple Circuit, explained slowly

A schematic is a map of paths

A drawing of a circuit tells you nothing about where parts physically sit, and that is deliberate. It shows what connects to what, so you can answer one question: can current get from here to there? Learn to read it as a set of routes rather than a picture.

Conventions worth knowing: signals are drawn flowing left to right, power is drawn with the positive supply at the top and ground at the bottom, and a long drawing is cut into sheets with labeled off-page connectors rather than wires running across the page.

The symbols

Part              Symbol in words                                       Watch out for
cell              one long line, one short; the long line is positive    polarity
battery           several cells stacked                                  total voltage marked beside it
resistor          a zigzag, or a plain rectangle on newer drawings       value and wattage
lamp              a circle with an X or a loop inside                   it is a load, not an indicator
switch            a line lifted off a contact                           drawn in its unoperated state
fuse              a loop, or an S, between two terminals                in series, always
circuit breaker   a switch with a hook or an arc symbol                 resettable, so no spare needed
capacitor         two parallel plates; a curved plate means polarized    polarized ones go in one way
inductor          a row of loops or humps                               a coil; also a relay or a motor
transformer       two coils facing each other, core lines between        AC only
diode             a triangle pointing into a bar                        current flows the way it points
LED               the same with two small arrows leaving it             polarized, needs a resistor
ground            three horizontal lines, each shorter than the last    the circuit's zero
chassis ground    a small hatched bracket or rake                       bonded to the metal case

Dots and crossings

A dot at an intersection means the wires are joined. No dot means they merely cross on the page and are not connected. Older drawings used a small hop over the crossing wire instead. Reading a missing dot as a connection is how a beginner convinces themselves a board has a short designed into it.

Tracing the power path

This is the skill the exam tests under the heading of troubleshooting, and the order never changes.

Step   What you probe                      Good                    Bad
1      the receptacle                      about 120 V AC          0 V: it is the outlet or the breaker
2      the cord, end to end, unplugged     continuity on all three OL: the cord
3      across the fuse, powered            about 0 V               full supply: the fuse is open
4      across the switch, closed, powered  about 0 V               full supply: the switch is open
5      the power supply output rails       the printed value       low, missing, or unstable: the supply
6      at the load                         the rail voltage        rail present, load dead: the load

The method behind it: walk along the path until the voltage you expect disappears. Whatever sits between the last good point and the first bad point is the fault. You are not guessing; you are bisecting.

Block diagrams

A block diagram throws away the components and draws each functional section as a labeled box with arrows between them: mains inlet, power supply, main controller, user interface, motor drive, motor, sensors back to the controller. It will never identify a failed part, but it tells you which section to probe, which boards talk to each other, and where the signal you care about is supposed to appear. For a device you have never opened, it is the right first page: read it, pick the section, then go to the schematic for that section.
